8 Abstract
9 Bidirectional typechecking, in which terms either synthesize a type
10 or are checked against a known type, has become popular for its
11 scalability (unlike Damas-Milner type inference, bidirectional typ-
12 ing remains decidable even for very expressive type systems), its
13 error reporting, and its relative ease of implementation. Following
14 design principles from proof theory, bidirectional typing can be ap-
15 plied to many type constructs. The principles underlying a bidirec-
16 tional approach to polymorphism, however, are less obvious. We
17 give a declarative, bidirectional account of higher-rank polymor-
18 phism, grounded in proof theory; this calculus enjoys many proper-
19 ties such as η-reduction and predictability of annotations. We give
20 an algorithm for implementing the declarative system; our algo-
21 rithm is remarkably simple and well-behaved, despite being both
22 sound and complete.
23 Categories and Subject Descriptors D.3.3 [Programming
24 Languages]: Language Constructs and Features—polymorphism
25 Keywords bidirectional typechecking, higher-rank polymorphism
26 1. Introduction
27 Bidirectional typechecking (Pierce and Turner 2000) has become
28 one of the most popular techniques for implementing typecheck-
29 ers in new languages. This technique has been used for depen-
30 dent types (Coquand 1996; Abel et al. 2008; Löh et al. 2008; As-
31 perti et al. 2012); subtyping (Pierce and Turner 2000); intersec-
32 tion, union, indexed and refinement types (Xi 1998; Davies and
33 Pfenning 2000; Dunfield and Pfenning 2004); termination check-
34 ing (Abel 2004); higher-rank polymorphism (Peyton Jones et al.
35 2007; Dunfield 2009); refinement types for LF (Lovas 2010); con-
36 textual modal types (Pientka 2008); compiler intermediate repre-
37 sentations (Chlipala et al. 2005); and object-oriented languages in-
38 cluding C♯ (Bierman et al. 2007) and Scala (Odersky et al. 2001).
39 As can be seen, it scales well to advanced type systems; moreover,
40 it is easy to implement, and yields relatively high-quality error mes-
41 sages (Peyton Jones et al. 2007).

56 However, the theoretical foundation of bidirectional typecheck-
57 ing has lagged behind its application. As shown by Watkins et al.
58 (2004), bidirectional typechecking can be understood in terms of
59 the normalization of intuitionistic type theory, in which normal
60 forms correspond to the checking mode of bidirectional typecheck-
61 ing, and neutral (or atomic) terms correspond to the synthesis
62 mode. This enables a proof of the elegant property that type anno-
63 tations are only necessary at reducible expressions, and that normal
64 forms need no annotations at all. The benefit of the proof-theoretic
65 view is that it gives a simple and easy-to-understand declarative ac-
66 count of where type annotations are necessary, without reference to
67 the details of the typechecking algorithm.
68 While the proof-theoretic account of bidirectional typecheck-
69 ing has been scaled up as far as type refinements and intersection
70 and union types (Pfenning 2008), as yet there has been no com-
71 pletely satisfactory account of how to extend the proof-theoretic
72 approach to handle polymorphism. This is especially vexing, since
73 the ability of bidirectional algorithms to gracefully accommodate
74 polymorphism (even higher-rank polymorphism) has been one of
75 their chief attractions.
76 In this paper, we extend the proof-theoretic account of bidirec-
77 tional typechecking to full higher-rank polymorphism (i.e., pred-
78 icative System F), and consequently show that bidirectional type-
79 checking is not merely sound with respect to the declarative seman-
80 tics, but also that it is complete. Better still, the algorithm we give
81 for doing so is extraordinarily simple.
82 First, as a specification of type checking, we give a declara-
83 tive bidirectional type system which guesses all quantifier instanti-
84 ations. This calculus is a small but significant contribution of this
85 paper, since it possesses desirable properties, such as the preserva-
86 tion of typability under η-reduction, that are missing from the type
87 assignment version of System F. Furthermore, we can use the bidi-
88 rectional character of our declarative calculus to show a number
89 of refactoring theorems, enabling us to precisely characterize what
90 sorts of substitutions (and reverse substitutions) preserve typability,
91 where type annotations are needed, and when programmers may
92 safely delete type annotations.
93 Then, we give a bidirectional algorithm that always finds corre-
94 sponding instantiations. As a consequence of completeness, we can
95 show that our algorithm never needs explicit type applications, and
96 that type annotations are only required for polymorphic, reducible
97 expressions—which, in practice, means that only let-bindings of
98 functions at polymorphic type need type annotations; no other ex-
99 pressions need annotations.
100 Our algorithm is both simple to understand and simple to im-
101 plement. The key data structure is an ordered context containing all
102 bindings, including type variables, term variables, and existential
103 variables denoting partial type information. By maintaining order,
